Subject: Production burst plan — primary region selection & fallback scenarios

Hi Ingrid / Amir —

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week. Per our implementation kickoff, I put together three burst scenarios for Helios' initial dedicated GPU pool and a couple of region/fallback patterns we recommend. The attached workbook (burst-scenarios-v1.xlsx) contains:
- Scenario A: single-US primary (us-west) with multi-zone bursting inside the region (low-latency).
- Scenario B: dual-region (us-west primary + eu-central warm-fallback) for DR and latency-sensitive EU traffic.
- Scenario C: multi-primary routing (regional routing at edge) for 24/7 global throughput.

Key asks from you:
1) Which scenario matches your anticipated traffic shape for Q4 (burst size in tokens/sec and peak concurrent requests)?
2) Any regulatory or data residency constraints that would rule out a EU warm fallback?
3) Contract/PO timing from procurement so we can align reserved capacity lead times (we note a 4–6 week provisioning window for committed multipool capacity).

Sean and Marissa — looping you for technical and CS handoff notes; please flag any ops caveats (autoscale guardrails, KV cache warmup expectations).

Attachments: burst-scenarios-v1.xlsx

Thanks,

Thanks, Stephanie — the workbook is exactly the level of detail we needed. Quick answers:
- For Q4 we're planning for an expected baseline of ~120k tokens/min with bursts up to ~900k tokens/min for limited windows (5–15 minutes). Bursts are very spiky tied to nightly processing and batch user peaks.
- Data residency: our EU customers' PII must remain in EU for logging/retention, but inference inputs can route through US hosts as long as logs/retention are EU-only. So a warm fallback in EU is acceptable if logs stay localized.
- Procurement: we're preparing a PO; expect to have an internal approval by 07/08. Will that still fit lead times?

Two clarifying questions:
1) How does Redwood handle prefix/KV cache warming across region failovers — is cross-region cache rehydrate supported or do we recommend a cold-start mitigation pattern?
2) For autoscale guardrails, can we set an enforceable soft cap (preferred) and a hard cap to protect our budget in case of unexpected runaway requests?

I'll also invite our procurement contact to the thread once the PO is ready.

— Ingrid

Subject: Re: Production burst plan — primary region selection & fallback scenarios

Hi Ingrid —

Short answers to your technical questions:
1) Cross-region KV cache rehydration: we do not replicate live KV caches across regions automatically. Recommended pattern: maintain a small warm read-replica pool in the fallback region (keep minimal KV prefixes warm via synthetic requests), and enable a prefix-caching policy so that common prompts are pre-populated after failover. We can provide an automated warmup playbook as part of Dedicated onboarding.

2) Autoscale guardrails: yes — we support both soft and hard caps. Soft cap triggers throttling with prioritized queues (best-effort bursts), hard cap rejects additional requests once the hard threshold is hit. You can couple that with a budget-alert policy that will automatically downgrade to a lower-cost model variant if spend exceeds X over Y period.

Operational notes:
- For your burst shapes (900k tokens/min), you should plan for an initial commit for 2x baseline and a 4x instantaneous surge buffer in the primary region to avoid queuing. We recommend reserving <redwood_sow_placeholder>  and enabling burst-burst-capacity for short windows.
- If EU warm fallback is needed, plan for a light-weight set of instances sized for prefix warmup rather than full parity with US primary.

I'll attach a compact topology diagram (pool-topology-proposal.pdf) to the next update; Marissa will draft the concrete rollout milestones and a risk checklist.

— Sean

Ingrid / Amir —

Attached is the initial SOW draft + a proposed rollout milestone table (sow-draft-helix-redwood-2026.pdf). Notes and proposed defaults:
- Default choice: Scenario A (US primary us-west, intra-region bursting) unless you need EU warm fallback for regulatory reasons. Scenario A minimizes cost and complexity and meets low-latency SLAs for US traffic.
- If you accept Scenario B (EU warm fallback), estimated monthly committed cost increases by ~28% (standby capacity + warmup runs). We included burst minutes per month assumptions in the SOW.
- Proposed milestones: PO confirmation -> capacity reservation -> staging warmup (2 weeks) -> production cutover (1 week) -> 30-day stabilization.

Action items for Helios: please confirm which scenario and whether the EU log-retention constraint requires full parity in EU or just log-only residency. Once we have that, Stephanie will lock the PO-ready SOW and Sean will schedule the staging warmup window.

Attachments: sow-draft-helix-redwood-2026.pdf

Thanks everyone — good to see the SOW draft. Quick decisions from our side:
- We will proceed with Scenario B (US primary + EU warm fallback) because of log-residency compliance for EU PII. However, we do NOT require full compute parity in EU — warm standby as described is sufficient.
- PO timeline: internal approval complete by 2026-07-08; expect to issue PO that week.
- Please include a clause for a one-time warmup assistance (2 weeks, runbook + synthetic traffic) and explicit billing lines for burst minutes and overage rates.

Marissa / Sean / Stephanie — can you confirm: will Redwood's automated warmup playbook include example synthetic requests and a measurement report at the end of the 2-week warmup window? We want a clear acceptance checklist.
